examples: Even though he knew it was dangerous, he pressed on.
Although this shop is small, it has a good reputation.
Although he is a student, he runs a company.
This tool is convenient, yet it is also easy to use.
Although she felt dissatisfied, she kept on working.
fields.explain:
Used in essays, reports, and objective descriptions to express a mild “paradox”.
The second clause should not be a command or strong volition directed at the listener (avoid giving orders). When you need to give advice, 〜ものの/〜とはいえ is more suitable.
“も” adds emphasis to the contrast; it can be omitted in formal language if the context is clear.

• Meaning: “although… (still)…”. States two contrasting facts that exist simultaneously.
• Nuance: more formal and objective than 〜のに; less reproachful emotion than 〜くせに.
• The first clause usually expresses a condition/limitation/disadvantage; the second clause is an actual fact that overcomes or contrasts with it.
• “でありながら（も）” is used with N/Na to avoid ambiguity and is more natural.
fields.notes:
• With Adj-i: “狭いながらも工夫がある” is a pattern for praising something that overcomes a limitation.
• “でありながら” can take a contracted form in formal academic writing: AでありながらB（である）。
• To emphasize a clear paradox, add しかし/それでも at the beginning of the second clause for more force.
meaning_vi: ～けれども（逆接(ぎゃくせつ)）
examples: 1. 子どもたちは文句をいながらも、後片付けを手伝ってくれた。
The children complained, but they still helped clean up afterward.
2. 残念ながら曇っていて、初日の出は見られなかった。
Unfortunately it was cloudy, so we couldn't see the first sunrise of the New Year.
3. 「私はもう10年も東京にすんでいながら、まだ一度も東京タワーに行ったことがないんです」
I've lived in Tokyo for 10 years, but I still haven't been to Tokyo Tower even once.
4. 事情はよくわからないながら、何とかして助けてあげたいと思った。
Although I didn't really understand the situation, I wanted to help you somehow.
5. この車は小型ながら乗り心地がいい。
This car is small, but it's comfortable to ride in.
6. 警察官でありながら飲酒運敵をするとは許せない。
Driving after drinking while being a police officer is unforgivable.
7. A氏は若いながらも古い習慣をよく知っている。
Mr. A is young, but he knows old customs well.
8. 初めて作った料理だが、我ながらおいしくできた。
It's the first time I've cooked this dish, but it turned out delicious, if I do say so myself.
9. 何度も練習しているのに、一向に上手にならない。我ながら情けない。
No matter how many times I practice, I don't get any better. I'm hopeless.
10. ・当然のことながら
Naturally.
11. ・いやいあやながら
Reluctantly
12. ・狭いながらも楽しい我が家
My home is small but happy.
13. ・細々ながら
Though only a trickle. meaning_vi: Although, however ⏐ explain: Expresses contrast, something contrary to common thinking or to what one imagined. ⏐ examples: 1. 悪いことと知りながら、盗みを繰り返した。
Although they knew it was wrong, they kept on stealing.
2. 「狭いながらも楽しいわが家」という言葉がある。
There is a saying meaning ‘our home may be small, but it is happy’.
mistakes: Using 〜ながら (simultaneity) instead of 〜ながらも (concession) → wrong meaning.
Na-adj/N attached directly to 〜ながらも: “便利ながらも” is possible, but with nouns you should use “Nでありながら（も）”.
The second clause gives a direct command/request to the listener → unnatural.

fields.connection: [result] + なぜなら(ば)・なぜかというと・どうしてかというと + [reason]
examples: I won't be participating today. That's because I'm not feeling well.
I'm against this plan. The reason is that the risks are too great.
I'm moving abroad. The reason is that I want to take on a new challenge.
We will be closed today. This is because there may be a power outage.
I recommend him. That's because I believe he is the most suitable person.
fields.explain:
Position: almost always at the beginning of the sentence giving the reason, right after the conclusion sentence.
At the end of a sentence giving the reason, からだ／ためだ／からである is usually used to complete the flow of reasoning.
More formal than だって; more neutral than というのは; more logical in academic writing.
Works well when answering an implied "Why?" after a statement that raises a question.
Avoid overusing it several times in a row; use it once to introduce the main reason.

• Used to state the reason/explanation for the statement in the sentence just before. Translation: "because; if you ask why...".
• Typical structure: conclusion sentence first → なぜなら＋clause giving the reason＋からだ／ためだ at the end.
• Nuance: coherent, argumentative; often seen in written language, presentations, and reports. Also used in conversation to switch into an explanation.
• Different from から／ので: なぜなら is a conjunction between two independent sentences; から／ので connect within one complex sentence.
• Often goes with nouns indicating cause, basis, or reason: 事情／理由／都合／ため, or a clause ending in からだ.
fields.notes:
• Often seen in argumentative writing, business emails, and reports: "結論。なぜなら根拠…".
• In formal language, ending with ためである gives a more serious nuance than からだ.
• If the reason spans several clauses, split it into a few short sentences, each still keeping the explanatory flow after なぜなら.
• Do not use なぜなら to state a result; use it only to give the reason for the previous sentence.
mistakes: Forgetting the ending that closes the reason: writing "なぜなら時間がない。" is incomplete; correct: "なぜなら時間がないからだ。"
Putting なぜなら in the middle of a complex sentence connected with から/ので → unnatural; split it into two sentences.
Using なぜなら for obvious information that raises no question → redundant.
Confusing it with だって on the JLPT: だって is too colloquial and cannot replace it in written language.

rows: Connects within one complex sentence; natural conversational nuance.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったから<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だ。
Gives the reason for the previous sentence
Two independent sentences; reasoning flow, more formal.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。なぜなら<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
Soft; used in both conversation and writing; close in meaning to なぜなら.
<ruby>延期<rt>えんき</rt></ruby>です。というのは<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>だから。
Very colloquial, sometimes used to make excuses.
だってお<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がないもん。

examples: Want to go to a café or something this weekend?
Someone like me still has a lot more studying to do.
Passing without even studying? No way.
There's no way I'll lose to someone like that!
Somehow you seem to be in a good mood today.
Places like Shibuya and Harajuku
fields.explain:
Soft suggestion: Nなんかどう？／行かない？ is suggestive, not imposing.
Humble:私なんか… to lower oneself; in written language, 私など is more polite.
Contemptuous:人なんか／あいつなんか shows disdain; be careful with the context.
Emphatic negation: ～なんか…ない／できるわけない, expressing strong emotion.
Filler: なんか＋clause, softens the affirmative nuance; said casually without much thought.

• Expresses examples/suggestions in a suggestive, casual way: "like…, sort of…".
• Softening/contemptuous nuance: placed after a noun to downplay its importance (self-deprecation/contempt).
• Used in negative sentences/exclamations to emphasize rejection: ～なんか…ない／できるわけがない。
• Very colloquial; avoid in formal texts or with superiors (it can easily sound rude).
fields.notes:
• In marketing/sales conversations, avoid なんか because it sounds unprofessional; prefer など／などの.
• Several なんか in a row in one sentence can sound hesitant; use it in moderation to keep the flow clear.
• It can also come before adjectives in spoken language: なんか嬉しい（somehow kind of happy） has a vague nuance. | Comparison: など (more formal, N4) / なんて (dismissive, exclamatory)
mistakes: Using なんか in a JLPT essay → lowers the formality score. Prefer など／とか.
Attaching なんか to the listener/a superior → sounds impolite/contemptuous.
Thinking なんか is purely for listing. In fact, it also carries an emotional nuance (belittling, negation).
A long AなんかBなんか chain makes the sentence messy; limit it to 1–2 examples.

rows: <ruby>寿司<rt>すし</rt></ruby>や<ruby>天ぷら<rt>てんぷら</rt></ruby>など。
Emphasizes emotion/evaluation more than なんか.
More neutral than なんか, less contemptuous.

examples: Lie to my parents? I just can't do that.
Me, becoming a representative athlete? I can't believe it.
fields.explain: ◎ 「～なんて」in 「ひとりで登なんて」means "as for ~ / the idea of ~", and leads to a negation or a feeling of surprise.

examples: In research on this problem, no one is as famous as Professor Takahashi.
In many regional cities, population decline has become a serious problem.
Modern industry was born in Europe.
In times of disaster, staying calm is more important than anything.
The graduation ceremony will be held at ○○ Hall from 10 o'clock.
Our company's cars are second to none in terms of safety.
fields.explain:
Used to open a paragraph/set the context: N + において(は)、〜。
In ceremonial emails, prefer におきまして for added politeness.
When talking about abstract topics (歴史/社会/教育…), において is more natural than で.
Not used to describe everyday actions: use で instead.

• Establishes the context (place/time/field) for presenting the main information.
• Written/academic style; used in reports, press releases, and theses.
• における used as a modifier makes the sentence concise and formal.
• Different from で: broader in scope, rarely used in everyday conversation.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～で (at/in).
→ ～において is more formal and often used in written language, news, and announcements.
2) Used for contexts “at…, in…, in terms of…”.
→ Not only places but also “within a field/event”.
3) Not suited to casual speech.
→ In conversation, ～で is usually more natural. explain: Used when talking about a time or a place.
A more formal usage than “で” ⏐ examples: 1. 大阪において、国際会議が行われた。
An international conference was held in Osaka
2. 結果はホームページにおいて発表されます。
The results will be announced on the website
mistakes: Using it in everyday sentences: × コンビニにおいて弁当を買った → ○ コンビニで買った.
Confusing it with the meaning “regarding”: × 料金において → ○ 料金に関して.
Dropping “における” when a modifier is needed: × 研究において成果 → ○ 研究における成果.
JLPT: Choose において over で for administrative documents/reports.

fields.meaning: In place of, on behalf of
examples: Today I will give the greeting on behalf of the department manager.
My older brother will attend the ceremony in place of my father.
Tablets are being used in meetings in place of paper.
Robots carry out dangerous work in place of humans.
The share of renewable energy is rising in place of oil.
On behalf of the company president
fields.explain:
Formal representation at the office: " Nにかわって ご連絡いたします" is very natural.
Noun form " Nにかわり のN":電子契約 にかわり の仕組み.
With replacement trends, the sentence is often passive/general: ～が使われる／注目される／普及している.
Not used simply for "taking temporary turns" (alternating). In that case, use代わりばんこ／交代で.
More formal than のかわりに; suitable for administrative documents and reports.

• Representation/on behalf of: person/thing B performs the action in place of A. Example: 上司にかわって説明する。
• Replacement (trend/innovation): B is replacing/has replaced A in function/use. Example: ガソリンにかわって電気自動車が普及。
• Nuance: formal; often used in announcements, speeches, and business writing.
• The agent is usually the replacing party (after にかわって), while A is the target being replaced.
fields.notes:
• In the "representation" meaning, it often goes with keigo: ご説明申し上げます／ご連絡いたします.
• In phrases about technological replacement, the kanji 代 is used for formality: ～に代わって.
• The topic being replaced (Nにかわって) is not the subject of the action; the replacing agent comes after it and performs the action. | Variant: ～にかわり; not used for simple replacement of objects
mistakes: Using a verb directly before にかわって → incorrect. A noun must come before にかわって.
Confusing it with "in exchange": ～のかわりに also carries the meaning of exchange/compensation; ～にかわって does not have this nuance.
Expressing temporary alternation with にかわって → unnatural; use 交代で／代わりばんこで instead.
Reversing the replacing agent: 人間にかわってロボットが… (correct), not ロボットにかわって人間が… if you mean robots replace humans.

examples: I have a few questions regarding the materials.

fields.explain: ◎ Indicates a target or topic; the meaning is the same as 「～について」. It is a somewhat stiff expression.
fields.notes:
explain: Preferred in work/official contexts: emails, announcements, reports, research papers.
Attach it directly before a noun as に関するN for conciseness and formality.
Add は after に関して to make it a topic emphasized for the whole sentence.
examples: 1. この問題に関して、ご意見を伺いたいです。
I would like to ask your opinion on this problem.
2. 日本史に関する本を探しています。
I'm looking for books on Japanese history.
3. 新制度に関しては、来月説明会があります。
Regarding the new system, there will be an information session next month.
4. 安全に関しての注意事項を必ず読んでください。
Be sure to read the notes regarding safety.
5. その件に関しては後ほど連絡します。
Regarding that matter, I will contact you later.
6. 環境政策に関して調査を行った。
A survey was conducted on environmental policy.
──────
1. ➀　事件に関して

meaning_vi: About …; regarding … (formal)
explain: Similar in meaning to ～について but more formal. Often used in written language and announcements; has the form ～に関する＋N.
examples: 1. 「申し込み手続きに関してお伺いしたいのですが」
I'd like to ask about the application procedure.
2. パソコンで環境問題に関する記事を検索した。
I searched for articles on environmental issues on my computer.
3. 議長は時間に関して厳しいので、絶対遅刻はできない。
The chairperson is strict about time, so I absolutely can't be late.
4. 「その件に関しましては、後ほどご説明いたします」
I will explain that matter later. explain: Used when talking about some aspect related to an issue ⏐ examples: 1. この問題に関して、ご意見ありませんか。
Do you have any opinions regarding this problem?
2. 農業に関する論文を読む。
Read a paper on agriculture
mistakes: Using に関して for an attitude toward a person: ×彼に関して優しい → ○彼に対して優しい.
Overusing it in everyday conversation makes sentences stiff; switch to について in casual conversation.
Wrong modifier form: ×環境に関して対策 → ○環境に関する対策.

examples: The farther north you go, the shorter the hours of sunshine become.
As the amount of data increases, the amount of computation increases as well.
As the traffic jam cleared up, the arrival time moved earlier.
Please proceed to the next step following the message from the person in charge.
Handle it appropriately in accordance with the law.
fields.explain:
Suited to written language, reports, and textbooks.
Clause A should be an axis of continuous change; if there are two discrete states, consider につれて/一方で.
The form “に従い” is often used in headings/procedure notes because it is concise.

• Expresses a covariant relationship between A and B (gradual, a tendency).
• Expresses doing B based on the framework of A (rules/instructions/plans).
• Clause B is usually a fact/rule; avoid commands in the “covariation” meaning.
fields.notes:
• In the meaning “follow/obey”, commands/advice can be used because they are instructions: 〜に従って提出してください.
• In the meaning “change”, avoid combining it with volition: × 〜にしたがって、〜しよう.
• The kanji 従 has the nuance “follow/submit to”, suited to legal and regulatory documents. | Formal variant: ～にしたがい
mistakes: Confusing it with につれて in terms of formality and naturalness in conversation.
Using it for instantaneous events: × 合図にしたがって走り出した → use と同時に/とたんに.
Mixing the meanings “follow” and “change” in one sentence causes ambiguity; keep them clearly separate.
